name: Wei Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers or government, and nothing you say gets linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I cycle in along the canal to a little agency on Station Road, five of us in an old mill office. We mostly do logos, jar labels and market-stall banners for small food makers: a cheese farm, two jam people, a hot sauce guy who changes his mind every week. I spend most of the day in Illustrator getting label text to fit round a jar without the barcode landing on the chilli.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part and the worst part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best part is going to the farmers' market on a Saturday and seeing my label on a shelf. Worst part is the pay, honestly. I'm on less than most designers, my girlfriend Ana is a teaching assistant, and between us we save maybe a hundred a month when nothing breaks. Something always breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a tool like the pen tool. I use one now and then to mock up a jar on a kitchen table so the client can picture it. I wouldn't post much, I'm not a big poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, it means my job's about as safe as it was, which isn't very. Graham, who owns the agency, keeps saying the food makers are squeezed by supermarket prices, so they squeeze us. Nothing changes means I still can't save and Ana and I still can't afford a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and maybe ask Graham for a small raise in the spring, since AI isn't eating the work. I'd learn the mockup tool properly so I'm faster. And I'd keep putting the hundred away, even when it hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit flat, because the hype going away doesn't make my rent smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said something always breaks. What broke last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My bike's back wheel in September, then Ana's phone. That was most of two months of savings gone. AI going away doesn't fix anything at my agency. The food makers still pay us late and I still can't save more than a hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the agency would you worry about, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Jess, who does the social media posts for clients. That's the routine stuff that even a so-so AI can churn out. I'd worry the posts get handed to a tool and Jess's hours get cut.

say: I'd say AI is **just a tool**, like the pen tool.
I'd mention I use it for **jar mockups** now and then, nothing more.
think: My job stays about as **safe as before**, which isn't very safe.
Squeezed **food clients** mean low pay and **no deposit** for a home.
do: Ask Graham for a **small raise** in the spring.
Learn the **mockup tool** properly to work faster.
Keep saving **a hundred a month** with Ana.
feel: Mostly **fine**, a bit **flat** because rent stays the same.
S0.quote: AI going away doesn't fix anything at my agency. The food makers still pay us late and I still can't save more than a hundred a month.
fieldNote: He's **calm** about AI here but carries **money stress** from low pay.
He spots that **routine social posts** are exposed, for a colleague rather than himself.
Savings vanish with **small repairs**, showing how thin the cushion is.

steps.text: Ask Graham (his boss) for a small raise in spring
Practise the jar mockup tool until it's quicker than Photoshop
Put a hundred a month into savings with Ana

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who made the art these tools learned from should get paid, and we need rules about it. I'd probably go to a union meeting for once. I'd tell friends to learn the tools anyway, because that's where it's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the agency goes from five to three, and I'm not one of the safe three. I'm still learning and the boss knows it. If the agency only keeps people who can talk to clients or fix what the AI gets wrong, I'm not either of those yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using AI every day for label drafts, so I'm the junior who's quick, not the junior who's expensive. I'd join the designers' union and ask what they're doing. I'd also look at the printing firm on the industrial estate, because someone has to run the label press.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. It feels like being told to run when I'm only just walking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd join a union and also learn the tools. Isn't that pulling both ways?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I don't think so. I can think the tools are built on stolen work and still need to pay rent. The union is for the fight, and the tools are for Monday morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ana cut first if your hours dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways, then the car share membership. Then probably the trip to see my parents at New Year, which would be the one that hurts.

say: I'd say artists whose work **trained the tools** deserve **payment**.
I'd tell friends to **learn the tools** anyway, because work is heading there.
think: I expect the agency to shrink from **five to three** people.
As a **junior still learning**, I'm not one of the safe three.
do: Use AI **every day** for label drafts to stay quick and cheap.
Join the **designers' union** and go to meetings.
Ask about running the **label press** at the print firm.
feel: **Anxious** but not frozen, like being told to **run** while still learning to walk.
S1.quote: If the agency only keeps people who can talk to clients or fix what the AI gets wrong, I'm not either of those yet.
fieldNote: He holds two views at once: **union fight** and **daily tools**.
He sees **print production** as a nearby hands-on fallback.
First cuts hit **family visits**, which he minds most.

steps.text: Draft every label with AI first, then polish by hand
Join the designers' union and attend monthly meetings
Ask the industrial estate print firm about label press shifts
Cancel the car share membership and stop takeaways

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs stopping or slowing by law, and the money it makes needs taxing. I'd be loud about it, which isn't like me. I'd be on every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my design work disappears in 2028. Two years is nothing, I'd still be learning to be good at it when it's gone. The print press is hands-on, so maybe three more years there, but then robots run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the print firm and take any shift on the label press. Ana and I would give up the flat and move in with her parents for a year to save. I'd sign up to whatever the union and the government put together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like a stairway that just ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does those three extra hands-on years mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years on the print press buys me time to save money, but it doesn't buy me a future. It's a waiting room, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ana that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're going to her mum's, and I'm sorry. She'd say her job's safer than mine, and she'd be right for a bit, because kids still need a person in the room.

say: I'd say AGI needs **slowing by law** and its profits **taxed**.
I'd sign **every petition** going, which isn't like me.
think: My design work **disappears in 2028**, before I'm even good at it.
The **print press** gives me three more years, then robots run it too.
do: Take **any shift** on the print firm's label press.
Move in with **Ana's parents** for a year to save.
Sign up for **union and government** support schemes.
S2.quote: Three years on the print press buys me time to save money, but it doesn't buy me a future.
fieldNote: He sees the **robot gap** as a **waiting room**, not a career.
His partner's **classroom job** may outlast his for a while.
He'd become **politically loud** for the first time.

steps.text: Take any shift on the label press at the print firm
Give up the flat and live with Ana's parents for a year
Sign petitions for laws slowing AI and taxing its profits
Register for union and government hardship schemes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years and no excuse. Governments should be setting up retraining and support now. I'd share that with anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be out of design before 2031, because the tools get good before the finish line. But five years is enough to get properly trained at something. I'd still be in my early thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an evening course in print production next year and get on the press part-time. I'd keep using AI for the design side while I'm still at the agency. Ana and I would push the deposit plan back and just save hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but there's a plan. That's different from the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of work do you picture yourself doing in 2032?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know, and that's what keeps me up. Maybe I'm running a press, and then in 2034 a robot runs the press, and I'm 35 and starting again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your view on the union change with more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gets more important, if anything. With five years, a union could actually win something, like a training fund paid for by the big AI firms.

say: I'd say five years means **no excuse** for doing nothing.
I'd call on governments to fund **retraining now**.
think: I'd be **out of design** before 2031 as the tools improve.
Five years is enough to **retrain properly** in my early thirties.
do: Start an **evening course** in print production next year.
Use **AI for design** work while still at the agency.
Push the **deposit plan** back and save hard with Ana.
feel: **Worried**, but having a **plan** makes it bearable.
S3.quote: Maybe I'm running a press, and then in 2034 a robot runs the press, and I'm 35 and starting again.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose design work** early, before the AGI date itself.
Five years gives him a **training window**, but the **robot date** still looms.
He thinks a union could **win a training fund**.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening print production course next year
Keep using AI for label drafts while at the agency
Delay the house deposit and save every spare pound
Push the union to demand an AI-funded training pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. I'd want schools and colleges changing now. I'd still say the profits need sharing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd have time to become a proper designer and then move into something that lasts. Maybe teaching design, maybe packaging production. I'd be 37 when AGI arrives, which is old enough to have savings if we're careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the agency and get better, using the AI tools more as they prove themselves. In two or three years I'd look at a teaching qualification. Ana and I would try for the deposit after all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy still, but I can breathe. It feels like a long road with a known bend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said teaching. Why does that appeal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana loves her job, and people still want a person in the room with kids. I like explaining things, I'm just not sure I'm good enough at design yet to teach it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about your job still worry you in the first few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because the steady stuff still happens on the way. Even with ten years' warning, the junior designers at my agency get squeezed long before 2036 arrives.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** if schools and colleges **change now**.
I'd still argue the **profits** need sharing.
think: I'd have time to **get good**, then move into lasting work.
**Teaching design** or packaging production could carry me past 2036.
do: Stay at the agency and **use AI tools** more as they prove themselves.
Look at a **teaching qualification** in two or three years.
Try for a **house deposit** with Ana after all.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to **breathe**, like a road with a known bend.
S4.quote: Even with ten years' warning, the junior designers at my agency get squeezed long before 2036 arrives.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him **plan a career move** into teaching.
He still expects the **junior squeeze** in the meantime, so he isn't calm.
His partner's job is the **model** he looks to.

steps.text: Use AI mockup and layout tools daily as they improve

Save toward a house deposit with Ana

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without question. What would help is a proper income while you retrain, and some of the money the AI firms make going back to the people whose work trained them. A union strong enough to make that happen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it does to the small clients. The cheese farm and the jam people can't afford much, but they used to pay a person in their town to make their labels. If they can make their own labels in a minute, they'll stop seeing that anyone made them at all.

headlineQuote: The cheese farm and the jam people can't afford much, but they used to pay a person in their town to make their labels.
portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old junior** designer making labels and logos for small food makers.
He uses AI now and then, earns **lower pay**, and saves about a hundred a month with Ana.
He backs **unions and rules** on training data, but still learns the tools for Monday morning.
He sees **label press work** as a short hands-on fallback and **teaching** as a longer one.
His mood moves from **uneasy** in a plateau to **alarmed** with fast AGI.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his design work ends before he's even good at it.
whatWouldHelp: A proper **income** while retraining, paid partly by **AI firms' profits**.
